newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik president says to meet opposition leader.
newsitem.headline: Tajik president says to meet opposition leader.

text.p: Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov is ready to meet the head of the country's armed Islamist opposition next month, Rakhmonov's spokesman said on Monday.
"According to our information, the opposition have accepted this idea," spokesman Zafar Sayidov told Reuters in the Tajik capital, Dushanbe.

The meeting with opposition leader Sayid Abdullokhi Nuri would take place around December 9, he said, somewhere in northern Afghanistan, a country where the opposition have had bases during the past four years of civil war.
Sayidov said the meeting would prepare the ground for a possible accord to be signed in Moscow on December 23.
He gave no details of this agreement and there was no immediate independent word from the opposition on their reaction.
Two previous planned meetings this year between Rakhmonov and Nuri never took place.
The mountainous republic, which borders Afghanistan and China, has been torn by more than four years of civil war.
Tens of thousands have been killed and many more displaced, thousands of them to Afghanistan.
Russia, which has thousands of troops deployed in Tajikistan to guard the borders and carry out peacekeping duties, has been pressing both sides for a deal.
Russian servicemen were killed in attacks in Dushanbe last week. As in previous incidents, which have claimed the lives of dozens of Russians, the Tajik government blamed the opposition.
Dozens of Russian soldiers in Dushanbe have been killed and injured in attacks blamed on the opposition.
The Tajik defence ministry said last Thursday its forces had fended off an attack by Islamist rebels east of Dushanbe.
But government military sources said fighting still raged in the same area, the Khaburabad Pass, some 300 km (200 miles) from the capital.
The pass straddles the only road between government territory in the west and its mountainous eastern half, which is largely controlled by the Islamic opposition.
Earlier this month, U.N. military observers said they were "gravely concerned" by a recent flare-up in fighting which flouts a U.N.-sponsored ceasefire reconfirmed last July.
